1.pericope_label: Now upon the first day of the week, very early in the morning, they came unto the sepulchre, bringing the spices which they had prepared, and certain others with them. And they found the stone rolled away from the sepulchre. And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus. And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments: And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee, Saying, The Son of man must be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and the third day rise again. And they remembered his words, And returned from the sepulchre, and told all these things unto the eleven, and to all the rest. It was Mary Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary the mother of James, and other women that were with them, which told these things unto the apostles. And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not. Then arose Peter, and ran unto the sepulchre; and stooping down, he beheld the linen clothes laid by themselves, and departed, wondering in himself at that which was come to pass.

schools.summary: Decline to harmonise the discrepancies and account for them instead: at such moments of terror and astonishment perception and memory are not always very definite in their reports, and each set of informants described what they themselves had seen. On the angels' question, prefer the marginal rendering — Him that liveth — and hold that it was enough to change the whole current of their thoughts, while allowing the words manifold applications beyond the primary one. Note that the direct appeal to the women's memory is peculiar to this gospel and shows what does not lie on the surface elsewhere, that they too had heard the prophecies of the passion; and that the messengers are called men, not women, their dazzling apparel described by a verb sharing the root of the word for lightning. Supply the rabbinic parable of the priest's foolish servant who hunted for his master in the burial ground and was told that no one ever saw a priest among tombs, on which Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh it is not the custom to seek the dead among the living. Then handle the reception: the word for idle tales occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and is applied strictly to the trifling babble of dotage, medical writers using it of the wild talk of delirium, while the verb for disbelieving is imperfect, so they kept on distrusting. Flag the textual question throughout — this verse about Peter and several other phrases in the chapter belong to the shorter Western text bracketed as non-interpolations.

Collect the ancient versions on the word for idle tales, which give dream and jest, and note that they looked on the report as mere deception. On the order of events, judge that the evangelist has inverted it, the running to the tomb having happened earlier, and read the notice as sharpening the apostles' obstinacy, since Peter had already seen the empty grave when he still despised the women's report. Note that the first day of the week is the third day from the death, so that the Scriptures and the Lord's own predictions are alike verified; and identify the first witness as the woman out of whom seven devils had been cast, a sincere penitent to whom he appeared first.

Make the sending a reversal of the fall: woman, once the minister of death, is now the first to receive and to tell the awful mystery of the resurrection, so that the female race has obtained both deliverance from reproach and the withdrawal of the curse. Note that when they found not the body they were distracted by various thoughts, and that it was for their love of Christ and the tender care they had shown him that they were thought worthy of the vision of angels. Add that Peter, being of more ardent feelings than the rest, anxiously put himself foremost and departed wondering in himself at how the linen clothes could have been left behind.

Set the errand in its practical frame: the devout women bought their spices once the sabbath was past and the liberty of working returned, but stayed away while night restrained them, so that coming very early manifests their great zeal and fervent love in seeking and finding the Lord. Note that the first day from the sabbath is what Christians are wont to call the Lord's day, because of the resurrection. Then report the perplexity about the hour, since one evangelist says very early and another the evening of the sabbath, and offer the solution that different parties of women and different appearances may be meant. Preserve too the reconciliation of the differing numbers of angels: one was seen sitting within an outer enclosure fenced off in front of the stone sepulchre, and two others were seen afterwards standing where the body had lain, who spoke to encourage their minds.

Distinguish what is mystery from what is revealed: the manner of the re-uniting of soul and body is one of the secret things, but the infallible proofs that he did rise belong to us and to our children. Read the women's errand tenderly — they came to anoint the head and the wounded hands and feet and to scatter sweet spices, as we strew flowers about the graves of our friends, only to show our good-will.

Set the whole chapter out in summary before commenting, so the reader sees the shape: the women at the tomb, the vision of angels, the report disbelieved, Peter's examination, the road to Emmaus, the making known in the breaking of bread, the appearance to the eleven, the promise of the Spirit, and the ascension from Bethany. Then turn the linen clothes into an argument: had the body been stolen, all the wrappings would have gone with it, since stripping it would have cost delay and answered no end, and the disciples would not have run such a risk for nothing. Note also that some of the women had not come from Galilee, and that one of them was the wife of Herod's steward.

debates.question: How are the differing accounts of the hour to be reconciled?

sides.position: Different parties of women and different appearances may be meant — the place has perplexed many
Do not harmonise: at such moments of terror perception and memory are not definite, and each set of informants described what they saw

debates.question: Was one angel seen, or two?

sides.position: One sitting within an outer enclosure, and two others afterwards standing where the body had lain
The question does not need settling; the accounts agree in the main thing, and the angel looked like a man while some remembered two

debates.question: Is the order of Peter's visit as narrated?

sides.position: No: the running to the tomb happened earlier, and the notice is placed here to sharpen the apostles' obstinacy
The whole verse is a Western non-interpolation and its standing in the text is uncertain

outliers.note: Alone reads the sending of the women as a reversal of the fall, that she who was once the minister of death is now first to tell the mystery of the resurrection, so that the female race obtains both deliverance from reproach and the withdrawal of the curse.
Alone holds that the narrative order has been inverted and that Peter had already seen the empty grave before the report was despised, turning a chronological remark into a charge of obstinacy.

13.pericope_label: And, behold, two of them went that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was from Jerusalem about threescore furlongs. And they talked together of all these things which had happened. And it came to pass, that, while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him. And he said unto them, What manner of communications are these that ye have one to another, as ye walk, and are sad? And the one of them, whose name was Cleopas, answering said unto him, Art thou only a stranger in Jerusalem, and hast not known the things which are come to pass there in these days? And he said unto them, What things? And they said unto him, Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, which was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people: And how the chief priests and our rulers delivered him to be condemned to death, and have crucified him. But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel: and beside all this, to day is the third day since these things were done. Yea, and certain women also of our company made us astonished, which were early at the sepulchre; And when they found not his body, they came, saying, that they had also seen a vision of angels, which said that he was alive. And certain of them which were with us went to the sepulchre, and found it even so as the women had said: but him they saw not.

schools.summary: Review the candidates for the unnamed traveller and conclude there is no evidence to guide us, while noting the ancient identification of Cleopas with Alpheus. On the village, cite Josephus, who records that after the fall of Jerusalem Titus settled eight hundred discharged troops at an Emmaus sixty furlongs out, and canvass the modern identifications; observe that the name is probably significant, connected with the Arabic word for a bath and so marking warm springs, like the Latin and French names for spa towns. Distinguish the name Cleopas from the similar name in the fourth gospel and derive it as a Greek contraction indicating Hellenistic and probably Alexandrian antecedents, which may help explain why this man's story reached one evangelist and not the oral teaching behind the others. Say that the failure to recognise him means only that they did not know who he was, nothing supernatural need be supposed, since he appeared in another form and they were not expecting him. Find a picture in the verb for their conversing, an old word meaning to throw back and forth like a ball, so that talk becomes a game of words; prefer the better text in which they stop walking, the adjective for their faces occurring nowhere else in the New Testament; and correct the familiar rendering of the reply, which should be not art thou only a stranger but art thou alone a sojourner. Then argue from the incoherence of the speech that follows: it is stated just as it occurs to the speaker, with little connection, hopes and fears mixed in, and this artless confusion is what a forger would never have thought to invent.

Rule out the suggestion that the second traveller was Peter, on two grounds: Peter was among the eleven to whom the two returned, and anyone who knows Peter must think he would have been the chief speaker rather than Cleopas. Suspect that they were going homewards, meditating a retreat and stealing away without taking leave, since the morning's reports had seemed to them idle tales. Then draw the note: it well becomes the disciples of Christ, when they are together, to talk of his death and resurrection, whereby they improve one another's knowledge and refresh one another's memory.

Note that though three of the four evangelists pass this over or touch it briefly, each was assigned his portion by the Spirit of God, so that what is not in one may be learned from another. Then insist on the emphasis the evangelist himself gives: he says expressly that their eyes were held, lest anyone think the features of the body were changed, so that the failure lay in the beholders and all suspicion of a phantom is removed. Draw from this a lesson about the senses generally — eyes and ears discharge their office only so far as power is communicated to them from heaven, and we ought to count it a daily favour that we see and hear at all. Observe also that though they were in doubt about the resurrection they still had reverence for his doctrine in their hearts, so that they were far from any inclination to revolt.

Report that many learned men ancient and modern took the second traveller to be the evangelist himself, that some old versions insert a name as though it were a person, and that one version says positively it was Luke, while another authority argues it was Peter. Correct the manuscripts that give a hundred and sixty furlongs for the distance, since Josephus assigns the same sixty as the evangelist. Say that the failure of recognition was nothing supernatural, the reason being given elsewhere that he appeared in another form. Then note that it was a laudable and common custom among the Jews to converse about the law on their journeys, and that these two had special reason to discourse of the law and the prophets after what had just happened.

sides.position: Peter, on the evidence of a later verse and of the apostolic list of appearances
Not Peter, who was among the eleven the two returned to, and who would have been the speaker
Probably the evangelist himself, as many learned men ancient and modern have held and one version says positively
There is no evidence to guide us

debates.question: Why did they not recognise him?

sides.position: Nothing supernatural: he appeared in another form and they were not expecting him
The evangelist says expressly that their eyes were held, lest anyone think the features were changed; the failure lay in the beholders
They were continually held from recognising him, the imperfect implying a sustained restraint

debates.question: Should the reply be rendered art thou only a stranger?

sides.position: No: art thou alone a sojourner, the adjective being predicate — hast thou been dwelling all by thyself?
The sense is that anyone who had lodged in the city a single night could not have missed hearing it

outliers.note: Alone names Peter outright as the second traveller and argues it from a later verse and the apostolic list of appearances, against three others who variously propose the evangelist, deny Peter, or decline to guess.

Alone derives the name Cleopas as a Greek contraction indicating Hellenistic and probably Alexandrian antecedents, and uses that to explain why this man’s story reached one evangelist and not the oral teaching behind the others.

25.pericope_label: Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken: Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory? And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. And they drew nigh unto the village, whither they went: and he made as though he would have gone further. But they constrained him, saying, Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent. And he went in to tarry with them. And it came to pass, as he sat at meat with them, he took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight. And they said one to another, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures? And they rose up the same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and found the eleven gathered together, and them that were with them, Saying, The Lord is risen indeed, and hath appeared to Simon. And they told what things were done in the way, and how he was known of them in breaking of bread.

schools.summary: Soften the rebuke by the word used: it is not the term forbidden in the sermon on the mount, which implies contempt, but one denoting weakness or dulness, belonging to a somewhat higher style of language and used elsewhere only by Paul; slow of heart means dull, slow to comprehend or to act. Note that the necessity urged is a necessity of prophecy, and that the very things about the death which disturbed them were the strongest proof that he was the Messiah. On the exposition, take beginning as governing the discourse rather than the sequence of books, and infer that the echoes of that lesson are to be found in the apostolic handling of Messianic prophecy afterwards. Then deal with the meal: call it strange that anyone should expound the breaking of bread of the eucharist, since he meant to disappear in the very distribution and the supper was over before it began, nor does it appear that any of them tasted a bit — or, on the other side, hold the meal so full of spiritual significance that one may anticipate the technical language of theology and call it sacramental for them. Report the textual curiosity that a copy reads not was not our heart burning but was not our heart hidden, and prefer the burning on the strength of the psalm about the fire kindled while musing. Note that the verbs for burning, speaking and opening are all continuous, and that he became invisible rather than leaving the room.

Take the feigning apart rather than excusing it: to feign means properly to form or put together, as a worker in clay is named from the same root, so that the Truth itself did nothing by deceit but exhibited himself in the body such as he already was in their minds. Because they could not be strangers to charity, with whom charity was walking, they invited him as a stranger to their hospitality — from which example it is gathered that strangers are to be not only invited to hospitality but even taken by force. Or read the whole episode as a lesson in that duty: through hospitality men may arrive at a knowledge of him, so that those who did not know him in the expounding of the Scriptures came to know him in the breaking of bread, since not the hearers of the law but the doers shall be justified. Note that he who is taught in the word and communicates in all good things to his teacher thereby holds Christ so that he should not go far from him.

Refuse to soften the reproof and enlarge its target: it was not confined to these two but meant to reach the rest through them, since he had so often forewarned them of his death and confirmed it from the prophets that he might as well have spoken to blocks and stones. Hold that a journey of three or four hours afforded time for a full explanation, and that he did not assert the necessity in three words but showed at length that he was sent to expiate the sins of the world by the sacrifice of his death. Insist that Moses and the prophets must go before as guides if Christ is to be made known through the gospel, against those who mutilate it by suppressing them. On the feigning, grant that insincerity of any kind is a sort of falsehood and that the example has been used to license lying, and answer that the Son of God was under no obligation to make all his designs known, and pretended here in the same manner as he had given himself out to be a stranger on the road. On the meal, report that most commentators took it for the sacrament and that it might be said with some plausibility that the Lord was recognised in the mirror of his own supper, but judge the conjecture to rest on no probable grounds. Read the burning heart as a grace felt at the time but only perceived afterwards.

Turn their backwardness into evidence: their very slowness to be persuaded is a strong proof of the doctrine they afterwards believed, since men so hard to convince would never have credited it without the fullest assurance, and they died on that evidence. Exclaim at what is lost, since a discourse in which all the prophecies of the incarnation, teaching, sufferings, death and resurrection were adduced and applied would have been worth preserving; no wonder their hearts burned. Deny that the eucharist was administered, there being not the most distant evidence of it, and call the meal a mere family one that ended before it was well begun; explain the recognition by his acting as father of the family in taking, blessing and distributing. Report the manuscript that reads veiled for burning, and the Latin version that reads blinded, without adopting either.

sides.position: Not hard: the word denotes weakness or dulness, not the contempt of the term forbidden in the sermon on the mount
Hard, and meant for more than these two, since he had forewarned them so often that he might as well have spoken to blocks and stones
Justly termed such, and their very backwardness is afterwards a strong proof of what they came to believe

debates.question: Was there insincerity in making as though he would go further?

sides.position: No: to feign means properly to form, and the Truth itself exhibited himself in the body such as he already was in their minds
The question misses the point, which is that through hospitality men arrive at a knowledge of him
Insincerity of any kind is a sort of falsehood, but he was under no obligation to make all his designs known, and pretended as he had in giving himself out for a stranger

debates.question: Was the breaking of bread the eucharist?

sides.position: No — strange that anyone should think so, since he meant to vanish in the distribution and it does not appear that any of them tasted a bit
No: there is not the most distant evidence of it, and it was a mere family meal
Most commentators held so and it might be said with some plausibility, but the conjecture rests on no probable grounds
It was so full of spiritual significance that one may anticipate the language of theology and call it sacramental for them

debates.question: Did our heart burn, or was our heart hidden?

sides.position: A copy reads hidden, on the authority of Beza and Heinsius, but the burning is preferable on the strength of the psalm about the fire kindled while musing
One manuscript reads veiled and a Latin version blinded, though the burning is to be kept

outliers.note: Alone declines the puzzle about the feigning altogether and turns the episode into a lesson on hospitality, that those who did not know him in the expounding of the Scriptures came to know him in the breaking of bread, since doers and not hearers are justified.
Alone of five voices takes the meal as sacramental, against an explicit denial from three and a considered rejection from a fourth who reports it as the majority opinion of his predecessors.

36.pericope_label: And as they thus spake, Jesus himself stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you. But they were terrified and affrighted, and supposed that they had seen a spirit. And he said unto them, Why are ye troubled? and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have. And when he had thus spoken, he shewed them his hands and his feet. And while they yet believed not for joy, and wondered, he said unto them, Have ye here any meat? And they gave him a piece of a broiled fish, and of an honeycomb. And he took it, and did eat before them.

schools.summary: Pin down what they took him for: the Jews distinguished angels from spirits and demons, a rabbi defining spirits as those for whom souls are created without a body being made for them, but the disciples probably meant no more than that this was not Christ in his own person newly raised but a spectre in his shape, himself still dead. Note that both words for their fear are strong. On the proof, observe that the verb for handle is the one used in the first epistle of John as evidence of an actual human body, and that flesh and bones tells against those who denied it — while cautioning that we are not to conclude our own resurrection bodies will have flesh and bones, since he was in a transition state and not yet glorified. Hold that the conditions must remain transcendental and mysterious, there being a real corporeity together with a manifest exemption from the ordinary conditions of corporeal existence, and point to the undesigned coincidence that what Thomas afterwards demanded was exactly the evidence given here. On the disbelief for joy, call it characteristic of this evangelist to analyse in this way, since as men sleep for sorrow so they may disbelieve for gladness, the thing being too good to be true. Note that the best old documents omit the honeycomb, and take the two foods as evidence of ordinary diet, fish being the staple and honey common enough to enter the diet of the poor.

Press a doctrinal consequence out of the moment: if there were no such thing as a disembodied spirit, would he not have corrected the error, whereas instead he confirms the category by saying that a spirit has not flesh and bones? Then list the proofs in order — they saw his body, heard him speak, handled him, and saw him eat — and say that in these things it was impossible for them to have been deceived. Grant that they did believe in some sense, since otherwise they would not have rejoiced, but hold that their excess of joy prevented a clear and rational belief; and say that he ate not from any need of food but to give them still further evidence.

Say that he condescended not only to be touched by his disciples but to eat with them, so that they might not suspect his appearance was imaginary rather than actual; and that after he had been seen, touched, and had eaten, lest he should seem to have mocked the human senses in any respect, he had recourse to the Scriptures. Note the force of when I was yet with you, that is, when he was still in the mortal flesh in which they also are, since he was raised in the same flesh but not in the same mortality.

Note the awkwardness of the sequence, since two verses earlier they had spoken of the resurrection as fully ascertained and now their senses are so struck that they think it a vision; acquit them of fearing enchantments, and judge them readier to believe that an image of the resurrection was being shown them by the Spirit than that Christ was present. Then turn the physical proof into controversy: since the body may be touched and has solid dimensions, the passage refutes those who would have it present where no mark of a body can be seen, for that would make it change its nature and cease to be what he here proves it is. Make the joy itself arise from faith and yet hinder it, and draw the warning that we should regard the vehemence of our feelings with suspicion even when their beginnings are good. On the eating, say that he had no more need of food than angels have, that he ate to convince them, and dismiss as curiosity the questions whether the food was digested or what nourishment the body drew from it.

debates.question: What did they suppose they saw?

sides.position: Not a spirit in the technical rabbinic sense, but a spectre in his shape, himself still dead
A disembodied spirit — and the reply confirms the category rather than correcting it
An image of the resurrection shown them by the Spirit, rather than Christ himself present

debates.question: What does flesh and bones establish?

sides.position: A real human body against those who denied it, though we may not infer that our own resurrection bodies will have flesh and bones
That the body may be touched and has solid dimensions, which refutes a presence where no mark of a body can be seen
A real corporeity together with a manifest exemption from the ordinary conditions of corporeal existence — the problem stays transcendental

debates.question: How could they disbelieve for joy?

sides.position: As men sleep for sorrow, so they disbelieve for gladness; the thing was too good to be true
They did believe in some sense, else they would not have rejoiced, but excess of joy prevented a clear rational belief
The joy itself arose from faith and yet hindered it — a warning against the vehemence of our feelings

outliers.note: Alone presses a doctrinal consequence out of the disciples’ mistake, arguing that had there been no such thing as a disembodied spirit the error would have been corrected, whereas the reply confirms the category.
Alone turns the invitation to handle him into eucharistic controversy, since a body with solid dimensions that may be touched cannot be present where no mark of a body can be seen.

he took it, and did eat before them

44.pericope_label: And he said unto them, These are the words which I spake unto you, while I was yet with you, that all things must be fulfilled, which were written in the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms, concerning me. Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures, And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. And ye are witnesses of these things. And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high.

schools.summary: Set out the threefold division of the canon: the law is the five books of Moses, the prophets comprise the former group of histories and the latter group from Isaiah onwards, and the psalms stand for the whole of the holy writings, of which the psalms were the most conspicuous portion. Add the rabbinic curiosity that wisdom has hewn out her seven pillars, meaning the seven books of the law, the book of Numbers being reckoned as three because two verses about the ark setting forward are counted a book by themselves. On the opening of the understanding, draw the lessons: that further truth will yet remove present mysteries, that our own prejudices are one cause of seeing so many, and that God only can open the mind. Suggest that the gift of prophecy conferred by the laying on of hands may mean nothing better than this same thing, that the minds of such were opened to understand the Scriptures. Identify the moment with the gift of the Spirit reported in the fourth gospel, while calling this evangelist's account vague because it came at second or third hand. Then trace the links forward: witnesses is the key-note of the second volume, the charge to wait in the city reappears at its opening, and the promise of the Father answers to the more definite promise of the Comforter recorded elsewhere. Note the loose construction in the participle for beginning, and take the promise of power as a garment put on, an old metaphor found in the poets.

Argue that this belongs to the day after the resurrection, on the ground that what the fourth gospel reports of that day agrees with the words immediately following. Hear in it an indirect reproof of their gross forgetfulness, as if to ask why they hesitate as though this were new and unexpected when it is only what he had frequently predicted. Then explain the opening of the understanding: he had discharged the office of teacher with little improvement on their part and now begins to teach them inwardly by his Spirit, since words are wasted on the air until minds are enlightened, and the word is a lamp shining in darkness among the blind until the inward light is given. Note that only now was it clearly discovered that the grace of redemption extends to all alike, since until the resurrection he was acknowledged as redeemer of the chosen people only, and that the priority given to Jerusalem preserves the covenant order. Separate the doctrine from its ground, insisting that repentance is no cause of pardon and makes no satisfaction, tears of repentance washing away no sin. Then hear Christ claiming divine power by undertaking the Father's promise in his own person.

Place the saying on the day of the ascension, and observe that little is said of the Messiah directly in the historical books, the prophecies and types being contained in Moses, the psalms and the prophets. Give the Jewish division with its Hebrew names, cite Josephus for a count of thirteen prophets and for the claim that the third division contains hymns and rules of conduct, and call that account imperfect. On the opening of the understanding, say they had light enough before to discern the Scriptures as the word of God and as speaking of a Messiah, but not enough to apply them to their own Master, so that the book may be received as revelation while its proper reference is discerned only by the light of Christ; even the plain word is a dead letter to the unenlightened. Speak of a veil taken off the heart. Then read the choice of city sharply: the first overtures of mercy were made to his own murderers, so that no sinner need despair. List the three purposes for which the promised power was to be given — a sanctifying comforter within, demonstration accompanying their preaching, and the working of miracles to confirm their mission.

sides.position: On the day after the resurrection, since what the fourth gospel reports of that day agrees with the words following
On the day of the ascension

debates.question: What does the third division of the canon comprise?

sides.position: The holy writings — Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Song of Solomon, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles
Psalms, Proverbs, Job and Canticles, on the authority of Josephus — an account that is imperfect
The whole of the Kethubim, of which the Psalms were the most conspicuous portion

debates.question: What is the opening of the understanding?

sides.position: The removal of prejudice by facts, so that what had confounded them could now be accounted for
The inward teaching of the Spirit, since words are wasted on the air until minds are enlightened
The light by which the Scriptures already received as revelation are applied to their subject
The gift of the Spirit reported in the fourth gospel as given at this same meeting

outliers.note: Alone supplies the rabbinic saying that wisdom hewed out seven pillars, meaning seven books of the law, Numbers being counted as three; and alone suggests that the gift of prophecy conferred by laying on of hands may mean nothing other than minds opened to understand the Scriptures.
Alone places the saying on the day of the ascension rather than the day after the resurrection.

themes: the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms

50.pericope_label: And he led them out as far as to Bethany, and he lifted up his hands, and blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, he was parted from them, and carried up into heaven. And they worshipped him, and returned to Jerusalem with great joy: And were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God. Amen.

schools.summary: Lay out the geographical crux in numbered difficulties: the same writer reports elsewhere that the disciples returned from Olivet, a sabbath day's journey from Jerusalem, whereas Bethany is put at fifteen furlongs, which is double that; and Josephus makes Olivet only five furlongs from the city while a sabbath day's journey is seven and a half. Grant all three statements and reconcile them by distinguishing the town from the district that bore its name; or simply place the spot on Olivet, near where the great discourse about the last things had been delivered, from which both Bethany and Jerusalem were in view. Recall Bethany as the favoured home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus. Raise the chronological difficulty honestly, admitting that this narrative taken by itself would leave the impression that the ascension followed within a day of the resurrection, and noting that the interval of forty days is stated plainly at the opening of the second volume. Then flag the two insecure clauses: the words about being carried up into heaven are wanting in some of the best manuscripts, and the words about worshipping him are absent from most of them, both belonging to the shorter Western readings flagged throughout the chapter; the parting verb means he stood apart and was gone. Where the worship is retained, argue that it was offered to an absent Saviour after he had vanished from sight, so that it cannot have been civil respect but was the first religious homage paid to him after he left the world — and if worship may be rendered to him, he is divine. End on the joy, which is the note of victory.

Read the place as significant: Bethany means the house of sorrow, and there the agony in the garden had begun, so that those who would go to heaven must ascend from the house of suffering and go by agonies to their joys; note that Zechariah had long since named the mount of Olives as the place where his feet should stand. Frame the whole by the errand: his design being to reconcile heaven and earth and to continue a days-man between them, it was necessary that he should lay his hands on both, and so pass and repass — having business in both worlds, he came from heaven in his incarnation to despatch his business here, and having finished it returned to negotiate our affairs with the Father.

Make the closing gesture an office rather than a courtesy. When men bless one another it is nothing but praying on a brother's behalf, but God does not merely befriend us by wishes, granting instead by a simple act of will what is good for us; and because he willed that men should have a familiar view of that grace, he appointed priests to bless in his name as mediators. Trace the line from Melchizedek blessing Abraham, through the perpetual law laid down in Numbers, to the greeting in the psalm, and close it with the apostle's rule that the lesser is blessed of the greater, so that the true and eternal priest must discharge in his own person what the law had enjoined on others. Then say that the reverence now paid was rendered not merely to a master or a prophet, nor to a Messiah half known, but to the King of glory and the Judge of the world; and that the continual presence in the temple means they attended the public assemblies at the stated hours, which is contrasted with the fear that formerly kept them hidden.

Reproduce the geographical reconciliation in full, numbered points and the Josephus quotation together, and credit it openly to the authority from whom it is taken rather than presenting it as your own. Then set the ascension in its evidential frame: it was forty days after the resurrection, during which the most convincing proofs had been given, to upwards of five hundred at one time; as in his life they had seen the way to the kingdom and in his death the price of it, so in his ascension they had the fullest proof of the immortality of the soul, the resurrection of the body, and his continual intercession. Argue that the worship was not civil respect, since acts of civil respect are always performed in the person's presence, and these men were too much enlightened to be capable of any species of idolatry.
